analysis.one_liner: Guarantees government-backed health coverage from birth to age 23 for every child born after 2008.
analysis.headline: Introduced on the final day of the Senate's 2007 session and sent to the Finance Committee, the bill never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Every child born after 2008 would be automatically enrolled at birth in a new Medicare-style public program called MediKids, guaranteeing coverage up to age 23, including prescription drugs. Families would pay an income-based premium through their tax return, capped at 5% of income, with very low-income families exempt and reduced cost-sharing for poorer families. Families could still use private insurance, Medicaid, or SCHIP instead, with MediKids serving as an automatic fallback whenever other coverage lapses. A separate report would propose progressive tax changes to fund the program as enrollment grows.
analysis.who_benefits: All children born after 2008 would be covered from birth without application forms or enrollment gaps, and their families would no longer lose coverage when a parent changes jobs, moves, or loses income. Low-income families (under about $20,500-$35,200 depending on family size) would pay no premium at all [S3]. Families between 150% and 300% of poverty would pay 75% or 50% less in copays and deductibles [S2, S3]. The bill's findings state that more than 9 million American children were uninsured and received less preventive care, with lifetime health and economic costs [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children born after 2008 and their families

how_it_helps.text: Automatically enrolls every child born in the U.S. after December 31, 2008 at birth, so coverage cannot lapse due to job changes, income swings, or moves across state lines [S3].
Requires a benefit package at least as broad as Medicare Parts A and B plus all mandatory Medicaid children's benefits and prescription drugs [S2, S3].
Exempts very low-income families from premiums and caps any family's MediKids premium at 5% of adjusted gross income [S3].
Provides a refundable tax credit limiting a family's out-of-pocket cost-sharing to 5% of income, protecting against catastrophic medical bills [S2, S3].

Bars states from cutting Medicaid or SCHIP eligibility or benefits for anyone under 23, and requires states to use resulting savings to improve services like nursing home staffing and inspections [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Families with MediKids-covered children would pay premiums collected through their federal tax return, phased down to zero for very low incomes and capped at 5% of adjusted gross income [S2, S3]. The general Treasury would cover program costs before premium revenue arrived [S3]. Because premiums cover only part of per-capita costs (the annual premium is set at 25% of estimated per-capita cost), the Treasury would also direct the Secretary to propose a schedule of progressive tax increases as enrollment grows [S2, S3].

drawbacks.text: The financing is deliberately incomplete: premiums cover only about a quarter of estimated per-capita costs, and the bill leaves the funding of the rest to a future Congress via 'a gradual schedule of progressive tax changes,' meaning families could not know what the program would ultimately cost them or whether the taxes would ever be enacted [S2, S3].

Coverage would phase in only for children born after 2008, so the more than 9 million children already uninsured at the time would not have been reached until the program's later years, if at all [S3].

Cost-sharing would be set to mirror the four largest federal employee health plans rather than being set at zero for most families, so insured families would still face deductibles and copays subject only to the 5%-of-income catastrophic cap [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise — that no child born after 2008 could ever be uninsured — is large and clearly designed for ordinary families, with strong protections for the poor. The design weakness is honest in the bill's own text: it defers the hardest question (who pays the full bill in future decades) to future Congresses, and it reaches today's uninsured children only slowly, one birth cohort at a time. A fair reading is that the benefit to children was real but gradual, while the funding plan was a sketch rather than a finished program.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the 110th Congress — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rockefeller introduced the bill on December 19, 2007, the final day of the Senate's 2007 session, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1, S5].
The bill's only actions after that were the sponsor's introductory remarks; the complete action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action ever scheduled [S5].
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died in committee with only two cosponsors [S1, S4, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo won. Private insurers kept their role as the default coverage channel for children, and the more than 9 million uninsured children the bill cited gained nothing; no one bore the cost of coverage or the taxes to fund it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so there is no roll-call record; the sponsorship itself leaned bipartisan, pairing a Democrat with an Independent and another Democrat.

industries.note: MediKids would have made a public program the automatic default insurer for every child at birth, competing with private plans for that role. But the bill also allows MediKids benefits to be delivered through private health plans run under Medicare Advantage-style rules, keeping private plans in the payment pipeline even under the new program.

Guaranteed coverage for all children means providers get paid for care that currently goes uncompensated when uninsured children visit emergency rooms and clinics, and the bill directs the Secretary to seek pediatric providers' input on benefits.
The bill requires prescription drug coverage at least equal to the standard federal employee plan of 2007, adding a large population of newly covered drug customers.

Beyond the family premiums, the bill directs Treasury to propose 'a gradual schedule of progressive tax changes' to fund the program as enrollment grows, putting the long-term financing burden on higher earners.
